description: Ultimate Laplace is a team of curious students who love space, math and building tools that make complex science easy to explore. We are taking part virtually from the Eindhoven local event.
summary:
Landing near the Moon's equator is easier: Earth stays in view and the Sun is seen for longer. The south pole is different. Communication with Earth is hard; ridges and craters make the terrain uneven; the low Sun makes it freezing cold; and a lander gets its power from solar panels. Because the terrain blocks the sunlight, choosing error-free landing coordinates is critical.

Triad is a calculation and interface tool built to solve these problems. It reduces the difficulties a lunar mission team will face, raises the chance of success with the right dates and coordinates, and finds alternative sites quickly when problems come up.

Landing at the south pole is much more dangerous than near the equator, and only a few countries have done it successfully. Triad calculates in advance, with clear and verifiable data, where and when a lander can land. What makes it different: it finds alternatives within seconds; its interface is simple for new users; its calculations, every 10 minutes over two years, agree with NASA's JPL Horizons within 0.00003°; users can enter their own coordinates and print the results; and the sunlight calendar and horizon view can be played live.
details:
What it does

Triad compares landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole. It shows, for any site and time in 2027 and 2028, whether a lander's solar panel is in sunlight and whether Earth is fully in view for direct communication.

  • Suggests sites. It checks 26,045 points from 84°S to the pole, every 10 minutes through 2027 and 2028, searches every 500 m around the 30 best, and lists the 10 best by the team's rule: Earth's whole disk must be in view at least 30% of the time; then the shortest longest darkness wins (values within 24 hours count as equal), then the most sunlight. Listed sites are at least 10 km apart.
  • Compares with NASA's candidate regions. For each of NASA's Artemis III candidate regions, it shows the best point inside NASA's outline. Four of Triad's 10 suggestions lie inside NASA's regions, although Triad chose them without looking at the regions.
  • Suggests a landing window: the 30 days with the most sunlight in which Earth is in view at least 30% of the time.
  • Finds alternatives within seconds. If a site cannot be used, it looks at nearby places, nearest first, from 50 m to 10 km away, for the same dates; if none qualifies, it moves the dates.
  • Shows the sky. A calendar of sunlight and Earth visibility through the year, and the horizon all around the site with the paths of the Sun and Earth, which can be played live.
  • Accepts your own coordinates, tells you if the place is inside a NASA region or already in the list, and prints a report.

How it works

  • Terrain: the NASA LRO LOLA south polar elevation map (20 m per pixel). From every point, the tool looks out in 360 directions up to 150 km and finds the highest terrain angle, taking the Moon's curvature into account. The observer is 2 m above the ground, the height of a lander's solar panel and antenna.
  • Sun and Earth: NAIF SPICE ephemerides (DE440, with the Moon's libration) give the direction of the Sun and Earth from each point every 10 minutes.
  • Visibility: the share of the Sun's disk above the terrain (a solar panel's power depends on it) and whether Earth's whole disk is above the terrain (needed for direct communication).
  • Web app: the browser repeats the same calculation for the chosen site; a test checks that it gives the same results as the Python code.

Accuracy

The Sun and Earth directions agree with NASA's JPL Horizons within 0.00003° (40 checks). The terrain map is read without a pixel shift (checked against Shackleton crater and a second LOLA map). Sampling the horizon twice as finely changes the share of sunlight by at most 0.17 percentage points. A first-time user completed 7 test tasks covering the whole app without help. Full details are in ACCURACY.md.

Benefits

Triad reduces the difficulties a lunar mission team will face, raises the chance of success with the right dates and coordinates, and finds alternative sites within seconds when plans change. Its simple interface also lets educators and the public see why the south pole is so hard to plan for.

What we hope to achieve

With this project, we hope to help overcome the challenges of missions at the Moon's south pole and to be part of carrying out these missions more safely and successfully. Thinking of the icy crater floors and the sunlit crater slopes, we hope that the idea that the best places for colony-style living on the Moon may be at the south pole will be developed and tested. We would be proud to be even a small part of this.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SpiceyPy) for the calculations; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app, with no outside libraries; pytest and Node.js for tests; GitHub for the code and GitHub Pages for the live app. Claude Code (SI) wrote the code, as stated in SI_USAGE.md. The team reviewed it in VS Code as it was written, found what was missing and asked for changes, for example clearer charts, finer horizon sampling and the ranking rules. The team and Claude Code tested it together, and the team checked the results in NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap.

Source code: https://github.com/ultimatelaplace/lunar-landing-site-navigator · Demo video: https://youtu.be/fUmWoWfzyVA · Triad is a student project. It is not made or endorsed by NASA.
